title: Blue Car
full_review:
A gifted high school student becomes involved in an increasingly problematic relationship with her poetry teacher in the emotionally complex "Blue Car" (Miramax).

Directed by Karen Moncrieff, the textured narrative, echoing Nabokov's "Lolita" and buttressed by strong performances, explores people's hunger for authentic love and its unavoidable obstruction by the frailties of human nature.

Eighteen-year-old Meg (Agnes Bruckner) has been adrift ever since her father abandoned their family years before, driving off in a blue car. Her home life is a vortex of dysfunction, where she must walk a daily tightrope between resentful anger toward her inattentive mother (Margaret Colin) and fearful concern for her disaffected, self-destructive younger sister, Lily (Regan Arnold).

Meg's solace is her poetry -- the only lifeline that keeps her head above the swells threatening to pull her under. Encouraged by her English teacher, Mr. Auster (David Strathairn), she agrees to enter a school poetry contest, which she wins. Her victory affords her the opportunity to compete in the national finals in Florida -- an option quickly shot down by her mother for financial reasons. Nevertheless, Meg persists.

Under Auster's tutelage, Meg delves into her inner landscape, exposing her most intimate feelings in an attempt to stoke the embers of her muse. Auster, himself harboring the private pain of a son's death and a troubled marriage, struggles to sublimate his growing attraction for his alluring -- yet emotionally vulnerable -- pupil.

The bottom falls out when Lily commits suicide and Meg's tenuous relationship with her overworked mother disintegrates. In an act of defiance, Meg storms off to the competition in Florida, stealing and then hocking her mother's engagement ring to pay for the bus ticket.

Once in the Sunshine State, she searches out Auster, who, serving as one of the judges, is there with his wife and teen-age son. Auster seduces Meg, his paternal assurances lulling her into a hotel room where he satisfies the unspoken desires he can no longer restrain. While the shared moment is consensual, it is devoid of any tenderness -- amounting to little more than rape.

Feeling betrayed by the one authority figure she trusted, Meg lashes out, using the only weapon at her disposal -- her poetry.

Though at times difficult to watch, the film avoids being exploitive. Moncrieff chooses to populate her world with emotional cripples, which in many ways honestly mirrors the human condition.

The narrative is awash in gray, its subtle characterizations defying convenient, black-and-white labels. None of the characters is totally good or bad; rather each is trying to do the right thing -- though their choices throughout are misguided, even repugnant, and often lead to tragic consequences. In a sense, they are all too human -- confused, flawed, wounded and longing for emotional wholeness and spiritual healing.

Even Auster, whose advances are undeniably repellent and raise questions of statutory charges, ultimately comes across as a pathetic shell of a man, creatively impotent, emotionally starved by a sterile marriage, thirsting for some genuine human contact or affection. His alienation, like that of the other characters, is caused by a weakness of will -- the byproduct of fallen nature -- a brokenness they can struggle with but not evade altogether.

The film also emphasizes the important role family life plays in the emotional well-being of its members, as well as the devastating psychological effects a fractured home can wreak on children.

Due to a sexual encounter and recurring rough language and vulgarities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
